Question 2774
A first year medical student is asked to account for the body's calcium reserve during a discussion of mineral balance. The discussion notes that bone serves several roles at once and that one of them dominates the body's handling of calcium. Which of the following is most likely the approximate proportion of total body calcium stored in the skeleton?
A. 25%
B. 50%
C. 75%
D. 90%
E. 99%
Answer: E. 99%
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Bone Tissue: Functions and the Five Shape Classes
Why this is correct:
The lecture lists storage of calcium among the four functions of bone and states that approximately 99% of the body's calcium is stored in the skeleton, which is why bone is treated as the reservoir that systemic calcium regulation draws on.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Far too low, and would make bone a minor contributor to calcium balance.
B. Half would leave an implausibly large soft tissue and extracellular pool.
C. Still well below the figure the lecture gives.
D. Close but not the value stated, and the point of the figure is that the skeletal share is nearly all of it.
Objective: Define the general characteristics and function of bone tissue, the different classifications of bones, and identify their component parts.

MSK / Week 15 / Bone and Cartilage Histopathology
Question 2777
A materials engineer collaborating with an orthopedic group tests cadaveric cortical bone and reports that the specimens resist being pushed along their long axis with high stiffness. The group then asks which constituent of the bone matrix accounts for that particular mechanical behavior. Which of the following is most likely responsible?
A. Type I collagen
B. Osteocalcin
C. Hydroxyapatite mineral
D. Glycosaminoglycan ground substance
E. Matrix water
Answer: C. Hydroxyapatite mineral
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Bone Matrix: Mineral, Organic and Water Fractions
Why this is correct:
The mineral fraction, roughly 60% of wet weight and chemically a calcium phosphate, is what makes bone stiff and gives it compressive strength, the ability to resist pushing.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Type I collagen supplies toughness and tensile strength, the ability to resist pulling.
B. Osteocalcin is the most abundant noncollagenous protein but is not what carries compressive load.
D. Ground substance is a small part of the organic fraction and is not the stiffening component.
E. Water is about 10% of wet weight and is not described as a load bearing component of bone.
Objective: List the general and specific components of bony matrix and identify the function of each to the properties of bone tissue.

Question 2778
A graduate student preparing a seminar on bone matrix is asked to state what fraction of the organic matrix of bone is accounted for by its single most abundant protein, and to name that protein. The seminar will go on to discuss how that protein determines the tensile behavior of bone. Which of the following is most likely correct?
A. Osteocalcin, about 90% of the organic matrix
B. Type I collagen, about 30% of the organic matrix
C. Type II collagen, about 60% of the organic matrix
D. Osteopontin, about 30% of the organic matrix
E. Type I collagen, about 90% of the organic matrix
Answer: E. Type I collagen, about 90% of the organic matrix
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Bone Matrix: Mineral, Organic and Water Fractions
Why this is correct:
The organic matrix is about 30% of the wet weight of bone, and 90% of that organic matrix is type I collagen, with the remainder being ground substance and noncollagenous proteins.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Osteocalcin is the most abundant noncollagenous protein, which is a much smaller share.
B. 30% is the share of the whole wet weight taken by organic matrix, not collagen's share within it.
C. Type II collagen is the collagen of cartilage, not of bone matrix.
D. Osteopontin is involved in the osteoclast sealing zone and is not the bulk protein of matrix.
Objective: List the general and specific components of bony matrix and identify the function of each to the properties of bone tissue.

MSK / Week 15 / Bone and Cartilage Histopathology
Question 2779
A laboratory treats a cortical bone specimen so that the mineral phase is removed while the organic phase is left intact. On testing, the treated specimen can be bent and even tied in a loop without breaking, but it no longer resists compression. Which of the following properties is most likely retained by the treated specimen?
A. Stiffness
B. Compressive strength
C. Toughness
D. Radiodensity
E. Hardness
Answer: C. Toughness
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Bone Matrix: Mineral, Organic and Water Fractions
Why this is correct:
Removing mineral leaves the organic fraction, chiefly type I collagen, which is the component that supplies toughness and tensile strength, so the specimen becomes flexible yet does not snap.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Stiffness comes from the mineral fraction and is lost with it.
B. Compressive strength is a mineral property and is lost with it.
D. Radiodensity depends on mineral content, which has been removed.
E. Hardness is a mineral property of hydroxyapatite.
Objective: List the general and specific components of bony matrix and identify the function of each to the properties of bone tissue.

MSK / Week 15 / Bone and Cartilage Histopathology
Question 2780
A 3-year-old child is brought to the clinic because of bowed legs and difficulty walking. The child has had limited sun exposure and a diet low in dairy, and the wrists appear widened on examination. A radiograph of the lower limbs is shown. Which of the following matrix abnormalities is most likely responsible for the appearance?
![Radiograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-bonehisto-015.jpg)
A. A genetic defect in type I collagen structure
B. Disorganized coupling of resorption and formation
C. Excessive osteoclastic resorption of trabecular bone
D. Defective osteoclasts with failure of resorption
E. Insufficient mineralization of bone matrix
Answer: E. Insufficient mineralization of bone matrix
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Osteogenesis Imperfecta and Osteomalacia as Matrix Composition Diseases; Bone Matrix: Mineral, Organic and Water Fractions
Why this is correct:
The radiograph shows bowing of the femora and tibiae with widened, poorly mineralized metaphyses, the appearance of osteomalacia or rickets, which the lecture attributes to insufficient mineralization, often from vitamin D insufficiency reducing dietary calcium absorption.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A type I collagen defect produces osteogenesis imperfecta, which fractures rather than bending.
B. Disorganized coupling describes Paget's disease, a focal adult disorder.
C. Excessive resorption describes osteoporosis, which does not bow growing long bones.
D. Defective osteoclasts produce osteopetrosis, with dense rather than undermineralized bone.
Objective: Identify the histopathology of common bone and cartilage disorders including osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, osteomalacia, osteogenesis imperfecta, and Paget's disease

Question 2781
A newborn is evaluated after a limb deformity is noticed at delivery. The radiograph obtained during the evaluation is shown. MSK / Week 15 / Bone and Cartilage Histopathology
Question 2782
Two children are discussed at a teaching conference. One has had several low energy fractures of long bones, and the other has not fractured but has progressive bowing of both legs. Both have abnormal bone, and the discussion turns to which matrix fraction is abnormal in each. Which of the following pairings is most likely correct?
A. Fractures reflect a mineral defect, bowing reflects a collagen defect
B. Fractures reflect excess osteoclast activity, bowing reflects absent osteoclast activity
C. Both reflect a mineral defect, differing only in severity
D. Both reflect a collagen defect, differing only in age of onset
E. Fractures reflect a collagen defect, bowing reflects a mineral defect
Answer: E. Fractures reflect a collagen defect, bowing reflects a mineral defect
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Osteogenesis Imperfecta and Osteomalacia as Matrix Composition Diseases
Why this is correct:
Collagen supplies toughness, so losing it makes bone brittle and prone to snapping, which is osteogenesis imperfecta. Mineral supplies stiffness, so losing it makes bone soft and prone to bending, which is osteomalacia or rickets.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. This reverses the two mechanisms.
B. Neither disease in this pair is defined by osteoclast activity; those are osteoporosis and osteopetrosis.
C. Only one of the two is a mineral problem.
D. Only one of the two is a collagen problem.
Objective: List the general and specific components of bony matrix and identify the function of each to the properties of bone tissue.

Question 2783
A 9-year-old is evaluated after a fall, and the radiograph obtained is shown. The reading physician is asked to name the structure that appears as a lucent line crossing the bone near its expanded end, and to state what tissue produces that appearance. Which of the following is most likely correct?
![Radiograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-bonehisto-024.jpg)
A. Metaphysis, composed of compact bone
B. Endosteum, composed of a cellular lining
C. Periosteum, composed of dense connective tissue
D. Physis, composed of hyaline cartilage
E. Marrow cavity, composed of hematopoietic tissue
Answer: D. Physis, composed of hyaline cartilage
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Macrostructure of a Growing Long Bone

The physis, also called the growth plate or epiphyseal plate, is a layer of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and the diaphysis during the growing years, and because cartilage is not mineralized it appears as a radiolucent line.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The metaphysis is the narrowing bony portion adjacent to the plate, not the lucent line itself.
B. Endosteum lines the marrow cavity and covers spongy bone.
C. Periosteum is the external covering and is not seen as an internal lucent line.
E. The marrow cavity is the hollow center of the shaft, not a transverse line near the end.
Objective: Define the general characteristics and function of bone tissue, the different classifications of bones, and identify their component parts.

Question 2787

Question 2796
A researcher culturing cells taken from the bone marrow of an adult finds that a single population can be driven down several different pathways. Depending on the medium used, the cells become osteoblasts, chondrocytes, adipocytes or myocytes, and the same population can also be recovered from periosteum and from endosteum. Which of the following cells is most likely the one the researcher is culturing?
A. Hematopoietic stem cell
B. Monocyte
C. Mesenchymal stem cell
D. Osteocyte
E. Bone lining cell
Answer: C. Mesenchymal stem cell
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Bone Cell Lineages and the Build, Crunch, Sense, Line Roster
Why this is correct:
Mesenchymal stem cells are described as giving rise to osteoblasts, osteocytes and chondrocytes along with muscle, fat and fibroblasts, and they are found in marrow, periosteum and endosteum.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Hematopoietic stem cells give osteoclasts, macrophages, lymphocytes and blood cells.
B. Monocytes are committed hematopoietic cells on the way to macrophages and osteoclasts.
D. Osteocytes are non-mitotic and do not proliferate or differentiate further.
E. Bone lining cells can become osteoblasts but are not described as giving cartilage, fat or muscle.
Objective: Describe the histological appearance and physiological processes of cells associated with the generation, maintenance and resorption of bony tissue.

Question 2801
An investigator adds a recombinant decoy receptor to a marrow culture and finds that precursor cells no longer fuse and no resorption pits appear on a bone slice. Question 2804
Two scanning electron micrographs of trabecular bone from different people are shown side by side at the same magnification. A student is asked which cellular abnormality would produce the change seen in the specimen on the right compared with the one on the left. Which of the following is most likely responsible?

A. Osteoclastic resorption that is too high
B. Osteoclasts that are defective and resorb too little

Answer: A. Osteoclastic resorption that is too high

Difficulty: Medium

MSK / Week 15 / Bone and Cartilage Histopathology
Question 2805
A young adult with a lifelong history of several low energy fractures and a long standing anemia is evaluated by an orthopedic service, and the radiograph obtained is shown. On the film the marrow space is encroached upon along the length of the bone, and the bone itself is uniformly dense with poorly defined modeling at the ends. Which of the following cellular abnormalities is most likely responsible?
![Radiograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-bonehisto-083.jpg)
A. Defective osteoclasts with too little resorption
B. Excessive osteoclast activity
C. A genetic defect in type I collagen
D. Insufficient mineralization of osteoid
E. Disorganized coupling with mosaic bone formation
Answer: A. Defective osteoclasts with too little resorption
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Osteoporosis and Osteopetrosis as Disorders of Osteoclast Activity
Why this is correct:
Osteopetrosis, or marble bone disease, is an inherited disorder of defective osteoclasts with too little bone resorption. The bone produced is abnormally dense and prone to fracture, and medullary canals can become obliterated.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Excessive resorption produces osteoporosis, with reduced rather than increased density.
C. A type I collagen defect gives osteogenesis imperfecta, where bone is not abnormally dense.
D. Failed mineralization gives osteomalacia, with soft rather than dense bone.
E. Disorganized coupling describes Paget's disease, which is focal rather than diffuse.
Objective: Identify the histopathology of common bone and cartilage disorders including osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, osteomalacia, osteogenesis imperfecta, and Paget's disease

Question 2809

Question 2812
An investigator blocks the ectoenzyme carried on the surface of matrix vesicles released by osteoblasts, using an inhibitor that does not affect the cells in any other way. Osteoblasts continue to secrete organic matrix at a normal rate and remain cuboidal on the bone surfaces, but newly secreted matrix fails to acquire mineral. Which of the following consequences is most likely at the tissue level?
A. Scalloped resorption cavities along trabecular surfaces
B. Loss of trabecular connectivity with normal matrix composition
C. Thickened trabeculae built from a mosaic of woven and lamellar bone
D. Wide seams of unmineralized matrix on surfaces lined by osteoblasts

E. Dense bone obliterating marrow describes osteopetrosis.
Objective: Describe the mechanisms of deposition of bony tissue, the maintenance, the turnover and resultant structural changes to bony tissue as well as the mechanisms of bone resorption.

A student is asked to sort the five osteocyte derived signals in the lecture into those that act on osteoclasts and those that act on osteoblasts, and then to say which of the osteoclast directed signals reduces rather than increases resorption. Which of the following is most likely that signal?

Reference: Osteocyte Signals That Control Formation and Resorption

Why the other answers are wrong:

D. Dkk1 is aimed at osteoblasts and decreases formation.

Question 2822
During growth, the diameter of a long bone increases as bone is added on the outer surface of the shaft while bone is removed from the surface facing the marrow cavity. Answer: D. Modeling
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Bone Modeling Against Bone Remodeling

Modeling is the independent action of osteoclasts or osteoblasts on different surfaces, uncoupled from one another, and it is the major determinant of the size and shape of bone, including long bone diameter.

C. Coupling is the link between resorption and formation that defines remodeling.
E. Interstitial growth cannot occur in bone because the matrix is hard.

Question 2828
A 53-year-old woman has had no menstrual periods for two years and her bone mineral density has fallen over that interval. Biochemical testing shows that both formation and resorption markers are elevated above the premenopausal range, with the resorption markers elevated to a greater degree. Which of the following most likely describes her remodeling balance?
A. Resorption increased above formation
B. Resorption unchanged above decreased formation
C. Resorption decreased below formation
D. Resorption below increased formation
E. Resorption equal to formation
Answer: A. Resorption increased above formation
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Unbalanced Remodeling in Menopause, Aging and Drug Therapy
Why this is correct:
During menopause the loss of estrogen signaling raises resorption, so more bone is resorbed than formed and bone is lost. The limb that moved is the resorption limb, and it moved upward.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Resorption outpacing decreased formation is the aging pattern, where formation falls rather than resorption rising.
C. Decreased resorption below formation is the bisphosphonate pattern and causes bone gain.
D. Resorption below increased formation is the teriparatide pattern and causes bone gain.
E. Equal resorption and formation is the balanced state, which does not lose bone.
Objective: Describe the mechanisms of deposition of bony tissue, the maintenance, the turnover and resultant structural changes to bony tissue as well as the mechanisms of bone resorption.

Question 2829

C. Serum fragments report formation and urinary fragments report resorption

E. Crosslinked fragments report formation and uncrosslinked fragments report resorption
Answer: B. Breakdown fragments report resorption and propeptides report formation
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Circulating Markers of Bone Remodeling
Why this is correct:
Resorption destroys mature collagen and releases telopeptides and crosslinks, while formation assembles new collagen and releases the propeptides trimmed off during that assembly, so the fragment type identifies the process.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. This reverses the relationship.
C. The lecture does not divide the markers by specimen type.
D. Type II collagen is a cartilage protein and is not part of this table.
E. Crosslinks are resorption markers rather than formation markers.
Objective: Describe the mechanisms of deposition of bony tissue, the maintenance, the turnover and resultant structural changes to bony tissue as well as the mechanisms of bone resorption.

Question 2844
A patient struck in the chest wall sustains a split through one of the costal cartilages and reports severe local pain, yet the damaged tissue itself contains no nerve fibers. Reference: Fundamentals of Cartilage: Avascular, Aneural and Covered

Question 2849
A biophysicist studying cartilage finds that the glycosaminoglycan side chains of the proteoglycan aggregate carry a high density of fixed negative charge. The investigator then asks what two separate consequences that fixed charge has for the mechanical behavior of the tissue under load. Which of the following is most likely correct?
A. The chains repel one another and occupy space, and they attract water
B. The chains attract one another and compact the matrix, expelling water
C. The chains bind calcium and nucleate mineral crystals in the matrix
D. The chains crosslink type II collagen into visible fibers
E. The chains bind chondrocytes to the surrounding collagen
Answer: A. The chains repel one another and occupy space, and they attract water
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Aggrecan, Hyaluronan and the Water That Carries Load
Why this is correct:
Anionic groups on the GAGs repel each other so that the molecule occupies space and acts as a shock absorber, and the same negative charge attracts water into a hydration shell, a gel-like sac of fluid that carries compressive load.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Like charges repel rather than attract, and water is drawn in rather than expelled.
C. Mineral nucleation in matrix is a bone process, not a cartilage one.
D. Type II collagen fibrils remain invisible by light microscopy and are not crosslinked into fibers by GAGs.
E. Cell attachment to collagen is the job of chondronectin.

Chondroblasts sit in the inner, chondrogenic layer of the perichondrium and produce a matrix of mostly type II collagen and proteoglycans. Once a cell is completely surrounded by matrix it is called a chondrocyte and occupies a lacuna.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Chondrocytes are the rounded cells deeper in the section, each enclosed by matrix in a lacuna.
B. Bone lining cells cover bone, not cartilage.
C. Fibroblasts occupy the outer fibrous layer rather than lying directly on the cartilage.
E. The osteogenic layer belongs to periosteum over bone.
Objective: Describe the histological appearance and physiological processes of cells associated with the generation, maintenance and resorption of bony tissue.

A histology examination presents a section through a flexible appendage, stained with a method that demonstrates one particular matrix component. The candidate is asked to classify the cartilage plate running across the field. The specimen is shown in the attached image. Which of the following is most likely the classification?
![Light micrograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-bonehisto-047.jpg)
A. Hyaline cartilage
B. Fibrocartilage
C. Dense irregular connective tissue
D. Woven bone
E. Elastic cartilage
Answer: E. Elastic cartilage
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Elastic Cartilage: Built to Bend and Return; Comparing the Three Cartilage Types
Why this is correct:
The matrix between the lacunae is filled with a dense, darkly stained branching fiber network, and the field is distinctly more cellular than hyaline cartilage with no obvious isogenous groups. Both features are what the lecture gives for elastic cartilage, and a covering perichondrium is present on each surface of the plate, which elastic cartilage retains.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Hyaline cartilage would have a homogeneous matrix with nothing resolvable between the lacunae.
B. Fibrocartilage would show thick parallel bundles with sparse cells in rows, and it has no perichondrium.
C. Dense irregular connective tissue has fibroblasts rather than cells enclosed in lacunae.
D. Woven bone has osteocytes in a mineralized matrix with randomly interwoven collagen, not a fiber network between chondrocyte lacunae.
Objective: Define the general characteristics of cartilaginous tissues. For specific cartilage types (hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage) be able to compare and contrast their matrix composition, functions, and location.

Question 2879
A student examines a high power field from a cartilage specimen and notes that something fills the matrix between the lacunae that she does not see on her trachea slide. She is asked which matrix constituent accounts for the difference. The specimen is shown in the attached image. Which of the following is most likely responsible?
![Light micrograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-bonehisto-044.jpg)
A. Type I collagen fibers
B. Elastic fibers
C. Type II collagen fibrils
D. Aggrecan bound to hyaluronan
E. Sharpey's fibers
Answer: B. Elastic fibers
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Elastic Cartilage: Built to Bend and Return; Collagen Fibrils Against Collagen Fibers in Cartilage
Why this is correct:
The lecture states that the elastic cartilage matrix is like hyaline, with type II collagen fibrils and proteoglycans, but that it also contains numerous elastic fibers which are visible by light microscopy as a dense branching network running between the lacunae. That network is what is added relative to a hyaline specimen, and it is what gives this tissue the ability to bend repeatedly and return to position.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Type I collagen fibers are the addition in fibrocartilage, and they form thick parallel bundles rather than a branching mesh.
C. Type II collagen fibrils are present in all three cartilages and cannot be resolved by light microscopy, so they cannot explain a visible difference.
D. Proteoglycan aggregates are present in every cartilage matrix and contribute basophilia rather than a discrete fiber network.
E. Sharpey's fibers anchor periosteum to bone and are not a component of cartilage matrix.
Objective: Define the general characteristics of cartilaginous tissues. For specific cartilage types (hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage) be able to compare and contrast their matrix composition, functions, and location.

Question 2881
A low power section through a tubular organ is shown to a student, who is asked how this particular cartilage can add new tissue at its outer surface. The specimen is shown in the attached image. Which of the following most likely accounts for growth at the surface of this structure?
![Light micrograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-bonehisto-041.jpg)
A. Chondroblasts differentiating within the covering layer and becoming trapped in the matrix they secrete
B. Chondrocytes already within the tissue dividing and depositing new matrix around themselves
C. Osteoblasts depositing osteoid along the outer border
D. Capillaries within the matrix delivering progenitor cells to the surface
E. Osteoclasts resorbing the surface so that it can be rebuilt
Answer: A. Chondroblasts differentiating within the covering layer and becoming trapped in the matrix they secrete
Order: Third
Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Chondroblasts, Chondrocytes and Isogenous Groups; Fundamentals of Cartilage: Avascular, Aneural and Covered
Why this is correct:
A densely stained covering layer runs along both surfaces of the pale cartilage plate, and the lecture describes appositional growth as cells differentiating within that layer and then becoming trapped in the matrix they have just synthesized, which adds tissue at the surface. On a slide this reads as a gradient from flattened cells at the outside to rounder chondrocytes deeper in.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. That describes interstitial growth, which expands the tissue from within rather than at the surface.
C. Osteoblasts and osteoid belong to bone deposition, and no mineralized matrix is present here.
D. Cartilage is avascular, so there are no capillaries within the matrix to deliver anything.

Question 2882
A student is shown a transverse preparation taken from the shaft of a long bone during a practical examination. She is told to ignore the cells entirely and to name only the repeating structure that organizes the whole field, since that unit is what the next three questions will build on. The specimen is shown in the attached image. Which of the following is most likely that structure?

A. The trabecula
B. The osteon
C. The basic multicellular unit
D. The diploe
E. The isogenous group
Answer: B. The osteon
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Compact Bone in Ground Section: Osteons and Lamellar Patterns
Why this is correct:
The field is filled with cylinders of concentric lamellae, each built around a single central canal, with angular interstitial regions filling the gaps between them. The lecture names the osteon as the main microstructural unit of cortical bone and describes exactly this arrangement of concentric Haversian lamellae around a Haversian canal carrying vessels and nerves.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Trabeculae are the struts of cancellous bone and form an open lattice rather than concentric cylinders.
C. The basic multicellular unit is the team of cells that carries out remodeling, not a visible structural unit in a finished section.
D. The diploe is the spongy core between the two tables of a flat bone.
E. Isogenous groups are clusters of chondrocytes in cartilage, not a feature of bone.

MSK / Week 15 / Bone and Cartilage Histopathology
Question 2883
A student examines a bone preparation from the teaching collection and notes that the architecture is beautifully preserved, but that she cannot find a single nucleus anywhere in the section even at high power. The specimen is shown in the attached image. Which of the following most likely explains this?
![Light micrograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-bonehisto-029.jpg)
A. The specimen was decalcified before sectioning, which dissolves nuclear material
B. Bone matrix is acellular once mineralization is complete
C. The section was cut too thick for nuclei to be resolved
D. The specimen was abraded thin rather than decalcified and stained, so the mineral survived and the cells did not
E. Autolysis destroyed the cells before the tissue was fixed
Answer: D. The specimen was abraded thin rather than decalcified and stained, so the mineral survived and the cells did not
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Compact Bone in Ground Section: Osteons and Lamellar Patterns
Why this is correct:
The lecture defines a ground section as bone abraded thin rather than decalcified and sectioned, so the mineralized architecture survives and the cells do not. What remains is pure geometry, canals, lamellae, lacunae and canaliculi, rendered in shades of grey or brown with no histologic stain, which is precisely what this field shows.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Decalcification is the route used to keep cells, since it softens the tissue so it can be sectioned and stained conventionally.
B. Bone is not acellular, and osteocytes occupy the lacunae visible throughout the field during life.
C. Section thickness would blur detail generally, but the lamellae and lacunae here are sharply resolved.
E. Autolysis would degrade the matrix as well, and it is not how teaching ground sections are produced.
Objective: Define the general characteristics and function of bone tissue, the different classifications of bones, and identify their component parts.

MSK / Week 15 / Bone and Cartilage Histopathology
Question 2884
A high power field from a bone preparation is shown to a student during a laboratory session. She is told that the preparation method has removed every cell from the tissue, and is asked to work out from the architecture alone which cell type occupied the small dark spaces scattered through the lamellae during life. The specimen is shown in the attached image. Which of the following is most likely that cell?
![Light micrograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-bonehisto-030.jpg)
A. Osteoblast
B. Osteoclast
C. Bone lining cell
D. Chondrocyte
E. Osteocyte
Answer: E. Osteocyte
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Osteocytes: Lacunae, Canaliculi and Mechanosensation; Compact Bone in Ground Section: Osteons and Lamellar Patterns
Why this is correct:
The spaces are lacunae set within the mineralized lamellae, and fine channels radiate from each one into the surrounding matrix. The lecture states that the osteocyte is the only bone cell completely encased in mineralized matrix, sitting in a lacuna, with dendritic processes running out through canaliculi to connect with neighboring cells through gap junctions.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Osteoblasts sit on the bone surface depositing osteoid, not inside the mineralized matrix.
B. Osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells that sit in resorption bays on a surface.
C. Bone lining cells cover quiescent surfaces and are also not enclosed in matrix.
D. Chondrocytes occupy lacunae in cartilage, which has no lamellae or canaliculi.
Objective: Describe the histological appearance and physiological processes of cells associated with the generation, maintenance and resorption of bony tissue.

MSK / Week 15 / Bone and Cartilage Histopathology
Question 2885
During a discussion of cortical bone architecture, a student asks why the tissue is organized into units of a fixed size rather than as one continuous mass. The field under discussion is shown in the attached image. Which of the following most likely constrains how large each unit can be?
![Light micrograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-bonehisto-030.jpg)
A. The number of lamellae that can be deposited before the collagen orientation repeats
B. The mechanical strength of the mineralized matrix itself
C. The distance over which nutrients can diffuse through canaliculi to reach the enclosed cells
D. The rate at which osteoclasts can tunnel through cortical bone
E. The surface to volume ratio required for mineral homeostasis
Answer: C. The distance over which nutrients can diffuse through canaliculi to reach the enclosed cells
Order: Third
Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Osteocytes: Lacunae, Canaliculi and Mechanosensation; Compact Bone in Ground Section: Osteons and Lamellar Patterns
Why this is correct:
The lecture makes this point directly. Nutrients reach osteocytes by diffusion through the canaliculi around their processes, which puts a ceiling on how far an osteocyte can sit from a blood vessel, and that constraint is one reason the osteon is built around a central canal. The canal carries the vessel and every cell in the unit must lie within diffusion range of it.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Lamellar collagen orientation alternates between layers but does not set an outer limit on unit diameter.
B. Mineralized matrix strength is a property of the tissue rather than the reason for the central canal.
D. Osteoclast tunneling through cortical bone during remodeling does not determine the finished unit's size limit.
E. The high surface to volume ratio belongs to trabecular bone and explains its role in mineral homeostasis, not the osteon's dimensions.
Objective: Describe the histological appearance and physiological processes of cells associated with the generation, maintenance and resorption of bony tissue.

Question 2886
A student examines a cartilage specimen taken from near the end of a long bone in a growing child. Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Chondroblasts, Chondrocytes and Isogenous Groups; Hyaline Cartilage: The Glassy Default

The chondrocytes lie in long vertical columns, each column a set of daughter cells generated by repeated division within the tissue with new matrix laid down between them. MSK / Week 15 / Bone and Cartilage Histopathology
Question 2890
A student is shown a section through the end of a long bone and asked about the bone compartment that occupies most of the field behind the articular surface. She is asked which functional role that compartment principally serves. The specimen is shown in the attached image. Which of the following is most likely that role?
![Light micrograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-bonehisto-072.jpg)
A. Mineral homeostasis, because its high surface to volume ratio allows rapid exchange
B. Biomechanical movement and protection, because it carries most of the skeletal mass
C. Hematopoiesis within the mineralized matrix itself

Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Cortical Versus Trabecular Bone: Mass Against Surface Area

The bone here is an open lattice of struts with marrow filling the intervening spaces, which is trabecular bone, and the lecture locates trabecular bone in the epiphysis and metaphysis. MSK / Week 15 / Non-Neoplastic Bone Pathology
Question 2891
A 68-year-old woman sustains a vertebral compression fracture after a fall from standing height. An iliac crest biopsy shows thinned trabeculae and a thin cortex, with increased porosity. The matrix that remains takes up mineral normally and there is no excess osteoid on trabecular surfaces. Which of the following aspects of bone strength is most likely the primary abnormality?
A. The organization of lamellar bone
B. The mineralization of newly formed osteoid
C. The quality of the collagen scaffold
D. The amount of bone present
E. The rate of endochondral growth
Answer: D. The amount of bone present
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Bone Strength in Non-Neoplastic Disease: Quantity, Quality, Mineralization, Architecture; Osteoporosis: Resorption Outpacing Formation
Why this is correct:
Bone strength depends on quantity, quality, mineralization, and architecture, and this biopsy isolates quantity. There is less bone, and the bone that remains is normally mineralized with an unremarkable matrix.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Disorganized lamellar bone with cement lines describes a remodeling disorder, not thinned normal trabeculae.
B. Defective mineralization would leave excess unmineralized osteoid on trabecular surfaces, which is explicitly absent here.
C. A collagen scaffold defect produces fragile low-quality matrix rather than simply less of it.
E. Endochondral growth is a childhood growth-plate process and has no role in an adult vertebral fracture.

MSK / Week 15 / Non-Neoplastic Bone Pathology
Question 2892
A 54-year-old man reports diffuse bone pain. A bone biopsy shows trabeculae whose cores are calcified but whose surfaces are covered by a thick layer of matrix that has not taken up mineral. The total amount of matrix laid down by osteoblasts appears adequate. Which of the following steps in bone biology has most likely failed?
A. Crystallization of calcium and phosphate as hydroxyapatite
B. Osteoclastic resorption of damaged bone
C. Osteoblastic production of osteoid
D. Coupling of formation to resorption during remodeling
E. Chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate

Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: The Four Coupled Processes Behind Metabolic Bone Disease; Osteomalacia: Osteoid Laid Down but Not Mineralized

Formation and mineralization are separate steps. Osteoid is being produced normally, so the failure lies in the subsequent crystallization of calcium and phosphate within it.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Failed resorption produces dense unremodeled bone, not uncalcified surface matrix.
C. Osteoid production is stated to be adequate, so formation is not the failing step.
D. Uncoupled remodeling produces disorganized architecture rather than a mineralization defect.
E. Growth plate chondrocyte proliferation governs limb length and is not involved in adult trabecular mineralization.
Objective: Explain how abnormal cartilage growth, collagen synthesis, osteoclast function, mineralization, and remodeling produce distinct bone phenotypes.

Question 2894

Question 2895
A 62-year-old woman is being evaluated for weak bones. Why the other answers are wrong:

Reference: The Four Coupled Processes Behind Metabolic Bone Disease; Osteopetrosis: Failure of Osteoclastic Resorption
Why this is correct:
Osteopetrosis is a disorder of osteoclast development or of the acidification and resorption machinery, so resorption fails while formation continues. That isolates the resorptive limb.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Osteogenesis imperfecta is a defect of the collagen matrix rather than of any cellular process.
B. Achondroplasia impairs chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate.
C. Osteomalacia impairs mineralization of osteoid that has already been formed.
E. Osteoporosis reflects an imbalance between resorption and formation rather than failure of one of them.
Objective: Explain how abnormal cartilage growth, collagen synthesis, osteoclast function, mineralization, and remodeling produce distinct bone phenotypes.

The specimen shows the medullary cavity obliterated by dense bone, which is osteopetrosis. The same failure of resorption narrows the foramina through which cranial nerves pass, producing compression.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Anemia in this disorder results from marrow crowding and does not demyelinate cranial nerves.
B. This is a non-neoplastic disorder, and tumour infiltration is not part of it.
C. Unmineralized osteoid accumulation is the lesion of osteomalacia.
D. The bones in this disorder are dense rather than elongated.
Objective: Recognize the hallmark clinical and morphologic findings of achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta, and osteopetrosis.

Question 2917
A 9-year-old boy with a sclerosing bone disorder has dense bones on radiographs, a mild anemia, and a history of two fractures. During a family discussion his parents mention that his grandmother has osteoporosis, and they ask how the two conditions are related, since both have been described to them as diseases of weak bone. Which of the following statements most accurately contrasts the two conditions?
A. Both result from excessive osteoclast activity at different rates
B. One is a disorder of collagen quality and the other of collagen quantity alone
C. Both result from defective mineralization of osteoid at different ages of life
D. One is failure of osteoclastic resorption and the other resorption outpacing formation
E. Both produce reduced bone density by different mechanisms
Answer: D. One is failure of osteoclastic resorption and the other resorption outpacing formation
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Osteopetrosis: Failure of Osteoclastic Resorption; Osteoporosis: Resorption Outpacing Formation
Why this is correct:
Osteopetrosis and osteoporosis are mirror images with respect to the osteoclast. One cannot resorb at all, while the other resorbs faster than formation can keep pace.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Osteoclast activity is absent or ineffective in the sclerosing disorder rather than excessive.
B. Collagen quality and quantity describe osteogenesis imperfecta, not either of these.
C. Neither condition is a mineralization disorder, since mineralization is normal in both.
E. Only one of the two produces reduced bone density, and the other produces increased density.
Objective: Explain how abnormal cartilage growth, collagen synthesis, osteoclast function, mineralization, and remodeling produce distinct bone phenotypes.

Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Case Challenge: Diffuse Bone Pain and Difficulty Rising from a Chair; Osteomalacia: Osteoid Laid Down but Not Mineralized
Why this is correct:

Question 2964
A 68-year-old woman reports aching in one leg. The affected tibia is enlarged and warm to the touch, and a biopsy is performed. The biopsy is shown in the attached image. Which of the following processes most likely produced this appearance?
![H and E micrograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-gap-231.jpg)
A. Failure to deposit hydroxyapatite into normally produced osteoid
B. Repeated cycles of resorption and formation that never align with one another
C. Absent osteoclastic clearance of the cartilage model
D. Resorption persistently exceeding formation across the whole skeleton

Answer: B. Repeated cycles of resorption and formation that never align with one another
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Paget Disease of Bone: Focal High-Turnover Remodeling; The Four Coupled Processes Behind Metabolic Bone Disease
Why this is correct:
Cement lines mark where a resorption front stopped and formation began. When those cycles repeat without ever lining up, the lines accumulate in every orientation and leave the mosaic seen here, which is why the bone is abundant yet structurally disorganized.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A mineralization failure leaves unmineralized osteoid on the surfaces, which is not present.
C. Failure to clear cartilage produces retained calcified cartilage in dense unremodeled bone, a different picture entirely.
D. Generalized resorption outpacing formation thins trabeculae rather than thickening and scrambling them.
E. A collagen defect produces fragile bone without cement line mosaics.
Objective: Explain how abnormal cartilage growth, collagen synthesis, osteoclast function, mineralization, and remodeling produce distinct bone phenotypes.

Objective: Apply key clues from a short clinical vignette to distinguish low bone quantity from defective mineralization and disordered remodeling.

Question 2983
A 7-year-old child has anemia and thrombocytopenia together with a facial nerve palsy. Radiographs are shown in the attached image. Which of the following best explains both the imaging appearance and the blood counts?
![Radiograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-bonehisto-020.jpg)
A. Bone that is never resorbed accumulates and narrows the medullary cavity
B. High-turnover remodeling replaces the marrow with fibrous tissue
C. Osteoid is produced but not mineralized throughout the skeleton
D. Osteoblast numbers fall while resorption continues unchecked
E. Prolonged vitamin D deficiency impairs erythropoiesis directly
Answer: A. Bone that is never resorbed accumulates and narrows the medullary cavity
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Osteopetrosis: Dense Bone, Narrowed Marrow, and Cranial Nerve Effects; Osteopetrosis: Failure of Osteoclastic Resorption
Why this is correct:
The failing cell in osteopetrosis is the osteoclast, so bone accumulates everywhere it is laid down. That same unresorbed bone crowds the marrow cavity, producing anemia and thrombocytopenia, and narrows the skull foramina, producing cranial nerve palsies.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Marrow fibrosis from high turnover is not the mechanism the lecture gives, and Paget disease is focal rather than generalized.
C. A mineralization defect produces lucent soft bone rather than the dense bone shown.
D. Falling osteoblast numbers with continued resorption would reduce bone mass, the opposite of this picture.
E. Vitamin D deficiency causes a mineralization defect and does not explain dense bones or a nerve palsy.
Objective: Recognize the hallmark clinical and morphologic findings of achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta, and osteopetrosis.

MSK / Week 15 / Non-Neoplastic Bone Pathology
Question 2985
A 9-year-old child has sustained two fractures after minor falls. A lateral radiograph of the lumbar spine is shown in the attached image. Which of the following best explains why these bones fracture despite their increased density?
![Radiograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-bonehisto-021.jpg)
A. A thick layer of unmineralized osteoid covers the trabecular surfaces
B. The trabeculae are thin and sparse despite the sclerotic appearance
C. The accumulated bone is poorly remodeled primary bone
D. Type I collagen in the matrix is qualitatively abnormal
E. The cortex has been replaced by fibrous tissue
Answer: C. The accumulated bone is poorly remodeled primary bone
Order: Third
Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Osteopetrosis: Failure of Osteoclastic Resorption; Bone Strength in Non-Neoplastic Disease: Quantity, Quality, Mineralization, Architecture
Why this is correct:
Remodeling is what converts primary bone into mechanically competent lamellar bone. When osteoclasts cannot resorb, that conversion never happens, so the skeleton is radiographically dense and mechanically poor at the same time. High bone density does not mean normal bone strength.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Unmineralized osteoid would make the bone lucent and soft rather than dense and brittle.
B. The density on this film reflects accumulated bone rather than a sclerotic appearance masking thin trabeculae.
D. A qualitative collagen defect is osteogenesis imperfecta, which produces osteopenic rather than sclerotic bone.
E. The cortex is thickened bone rather than fibrous tissue.
Objective: Recognize the hallmark clinical and morphologic findings of achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta, and osteopetrosis.

D. Both are open because both involve more than one fragment
E. Neither can be classified without knowing the direction of the fracture line
Answer: A. The first is simple and open, the second is comminuted and closed
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Counting the fragments: simple and comminuted; Fractures that communicate with the atmosphere
Why this is correct:
Fragment count and communication with the atmosphere are independent classifications. Two fragments make a fracture simple, and a wound that exposes the bone makes it open, while five fragments make a fracture comminuted and intact skin makes it closed.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The fragment counts are reversed.
C. Both the fragment counts and the skin status are reversed.
D. Fragment number has nothing to do with whether a fracture communicates with outside air.
E. Both classifications can be made without knowing the direction of the fracture line.
Objective: Describe the sequence and timing of events in the repair of a bony fracture

Question 3108
A 68-year-old woman slips on ice and lands on her outstretched hand with the forearm pronated and the wrist forced backward. She presents with wrist pain and a visible step deformity on the back of the wrist. Which of the following is the most likely injury?
A. Subluxation of the radial head
B. Complete transverse fracture of the distal radius
C. Rupture of the triangular fibrocartilage complex
D. Fracture of the olecranon of the ulna
E. Tear of the ulnar collateral ligament of the elbow
Answer: B. Complete transverse fracture of the distal radius
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Colles fracture of the distal radius
Why this is correct:
A Colles fracture is a complete transverse fracture of the distal radius produced by forced dorsiflexion of the hand with the forearm and hand pronated, which is the fall on an outstretched hand.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Radial head subluxation follows sudden traction on a pronated limb in a child, not a fall on the hand.
C. The triangular fibrocartilage complex binds the distal radius and ulna but is not what this mechanism fractures.
D. The olecranon is at the elbow, away from the site of loading in this mechanism.
E. The ulnar collateral ligament is a medial elbow structure and would not produce a deformity at the wrist.
Objective: Identify the bony features, articulations, and associated ligaments of the distal humerus, as well as the radius and ulna. Discuss the anatomical & clinical considerations of fractures of these bones, radial head subluxation, and elbow dislocation.

A patient has a joint at the elbow fused surgically after trauma. Afterward she can still flex and extend the elbow normally but can no longer turn the palm from facing up to facing down. Which of the following joints was most likely fused?
A. The humero-ulnar articulation between the trochlea and the trochlear notch

C. The syndesmosis along the shafts is the fibrous joint of the interosseous membrane, not the pivot.
D. The capitulum articulates with the head of the radius, not with the coronoid process.
E. The ulna does not reach the carpus, so no such articulation exists.

Question 3132
A 38-year-old woman has an injury that destroys one muscle in the proximal forearm. Afterward she retains some ability to turn the palm downward but has lost a contribution to elbow flexion at the same time. Which of the following muscles was most likely lost?

Pronator teres both pronates and flexes the forearm, so losing it removes a flexor of the elbow as well as a pronator. Pronation is only reduced rather than abolished because pronator quadratus remains.

A 52-year-old recreational golfer has several months of aching at the inner side of the elbow. He is tender over a single bony point, and the pain is reproduced by resisted wrist flexion but not by resisted wrist extension. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Answer: B. Medial epicondylitis

Difficulty: Easy

Medial epicondylitis is an overuse injury of the common flexor tendon at the medial epicondyle developing during repeated wrist flexion, which matches the tender point and the provoking movement.
Why the other answers are wrong:

D. Radial head subluxation is an acute traction injury of childhood.
E. An ulnar collateral ligament rupture would show instability on valgus stress rather than pain on resisted wrist flexion.

Answer: B. Medial and lateral cords, C5 to C8 and T1
Order: First
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Median nerve in the forearm
Why this is correct:
The lecture gives the median nerve as arising from the medial and lateral cords with a root value of C5 through C8 and T1, which is why it spans the whole plexus.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Medial cord with C7 to C8 and T1 is the ulnar nerve.
C. The median nerve does not come from the lateral cord alone.
D. The median nerve is not a posterior cord branch.
E. The median nerve draws from two cords, not from the medial cord alone.
Objective: Describe the course and innervations (i.e., muscular and cutaneous innervation) of the median, and ulnar nerves within the forearm. Describe common sites of injury and clinical manifestations of the subsequent neurodeficiencies.

MSK / Week 15 / Anterior Forearm and Elbow
Question 3168
A 41-year-old machinist whose work requires repeated forceful pronation develops aching in the proximal forearm with sensory and motor symptoms in the median distribution. Which of the following is the most likely site of compression?

B. On the anterior surface of the interosseous membrane

Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Common sites of median nerve injury; Pronator teres

Compression of the median nerve as it passes between the two heads of pronator teres is pronator syndrome, and the proximal forearm location and the pronation-heavy work both fit.
Why the other answers are wrong:

E. The annular ligament surrounds the radial head and is not a median nerve site.

MSK / Week 15 / Anterior Forearm and Elbow
Question 3169
Two patients each have a median nerve lesion, one at the elbow and one at the flexor retinaculum. Which of the following best explains why the forearm muscles are weak in the first patient and not in the second?

Difficulty: Medium

C. The ulnar nerve supplies only its own two muscles and does not take over.
D. The anterior interosseous nerve branches in the forearm, well proximal to the wrist.
E. The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm is sensory.

B. The ulnar artery, giving the radial recurrent artery
C. The radial artery, giving the ulnar recurrent arteries
D. The ulnar artery, giving the common interosseous artery
E. The ulnar artery, giving the posterior interosseous artery directly
Answer: D. The ulnar artery, giving the common interosseous artery
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Interosseous and recurrent branches in the forearm
Why this is correct:
The ulnar artery gives the ulnar recurrent arteries and the common interosseous artery, and it is the common interosseous that then divides into the anterior and posterior interosseous arteries. The radial artery contributes only a recurrent branch.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The common interosseous artery arises from the ulnar artery.
B. The radial recurrent artery is a branch of the radial artery.
C. The ulnar recurrent arteries come from the ulnar artery.
E. The posterior interosseous artery arises from the common interosseous trunk, not directly from the ulnar artery.
Objective: Trace the courses of the major arteries, superficial & deep veins, and lymphatics within the anterior forearm. Define collateral circulation, and describe why it is important at joints in general and specifically at the elbow. Identify sites where a pulse rate can be measured.

Question 3200

Answer: B. Head of the ulna with the ulnar notch of the radius

Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Distal radio-ulnar joint and the triangular fibrocartilage complex; The anterior forearm and elbow on radiographs
Why this is correct:
At the distal end the arrangement is the reverse of the elbow. The head belongs to the ulna and the notch belongs to the radius, so the head of the ulna sits in the ulnar notch of the radius. The radius then carries the hand around the relatively fixed ulnar head during pronation and supination.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. That is the proximal radio-ulnar joint at the elbow, where the head and notch belong to the opposite bones.
C. The radial styloid takes part in the wrist joint with the scaphoid rather than forming the radio-ulnar articulation.
D. The ulna does not reach the carpus, which is why the triangular fibrocartilage complex fills that gap.
E. The trochlear notch articulates with the humerus at the elbow and has nothing to do with the wrist.
Objective: Identify anatomical structures associated with the anterior forearm and elbow on X-Rays, MRI, and CT scans.

The ulna does not directly articulate with any carpal bone. The triangular fibrocartilage complex, which is the articular disc of the distal radio-ulnar joint, lies between the head of the ulna and the triquetrum and is the structure that transmits and distributes load from the hand to the ulna.

C. It limits extension and runs from the radius to the carpus, bypassing the ulna.

Question 3213
A 33-year-old man catches his hand in machinery and his wrist is forced into extreme ulnar deviation. He is later found to have an isolated ligament tear on the opposite side of the joint from the direction of displacement. Which of the following ligaments was most likely torn?

Question 3216
A 24-year-old woman is seen four days after a fall on an outstretched hand. She was initially diagnosed with a wrist sprain. She now reports numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers, and she cannot oppose the thumb. Sensation over the central palm is normal. Which of the following best explains her new findings?
A. Laceration of the recurrent branch of the median nerve
B. Compression of the ulnar nerve in the ulnar canal
C. Anterior displacement of the lunate compressing the median nerve
D. Avascular necrosis of the scaphoid
E. Traction injury to the median nerve at the elbow

Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Wrist Sprains and Scapholunate Ligament Injury; Anterior Dislocation of the Lunate; Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
Why this is correct:
Scapholunate ligament damage can force the lunate to dislocate anteriorly into the floor of the carpal tunnel, where it compresses the median nerve. Sparing of the central palm confirms the lesion is inside the tunnel, because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to it.

B. That would numb the medial one and a half digits and spare the thumb.
D. That causes lateral wrist pain rather than a median nerve deficit.
E. That would also weaken forearm flexors and pronators, which are not described.
Objective: Discuss the clinical presentation and anatomical basis for significant hand/wrist problems including: fractures, dislocations, lacerations, ischemia, tenosynovitis, and neurological injuries.

Objective: Discuss the fascial structures of the hand & wrist. Describe the carpal tunnel and ulnar canal, including the structures that course through each. Explain the clinical presentation and anatomical basis for Dupuytren's contracture, carpal tunnel syndrome, and ulnar canal syndrome.

Question 3230
A 58-year-old woman has arthritis limited to a single joint at the base of her thumb. She has lost flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and circumduction at that joint, a range no other carpometacarpal joint provides. Which of the following joint types is most likely affected?

Question 3231
A 37-year-old man lacerates the palmar aspect of his middle finger and afterwards cannot flex the distal interphalangeal joint, although he can still flex the proximal interphalangeal joint. Which of the following tendons was most likely divided?

Question 3236

Question 3237
A 39-year-old cook sustains a shallow cut across the fleshy bulge at the base of her thumb while opening a box. The wound is closed in the emergency department. A 63-year-old man comes to the clinic because his right hand will not open fully. He first noticed a firm lump in the palm two years ago. He has no pain and no numbness. The hand is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Question 3243

Question 3250
A physician explains to a patient that several different conditions can all produce the same median nerve symptoms at the wrist. Which of the following best describes the common mechanism?
A. Any lesion that stretches the flexor retinaculum beyond its elastic limit
B. Any lesion that reduces the size of the tunnel or increases the size of its contents
C. Any lesion that interrupts the blood supply of the median nerve in the forearm
D. Any lesion that thickens the palmar aponeurosis distal to the retinaculum
E. Any lesion that compresses the nerve as it passes between the heads of pronator teres
Answer: B. Any lesion that reduces the size of the tunnel or increases the size of its contents
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
Why this is correct:
Carpal tunnel syndrome results from a lesion reducing the size of the tunnel or increasing the size of its contents, such as inflammation of the tendons or their synovial sheaths, or an anteriorly displaced lunate pressing in from the floor.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Stretching the roof would enlarge rather than narrow the space.
C. The lecture describes mechanical compression within the tunnel rather than a forearm vascular cause.
D. That mechanism describes Dupuytren contracture rather than carpal tunnel syndrome.
E. That is pronator syndrome, which occurs at the elbow rather than the wrist.
Objective: Discuss the fascial structures of the hand & wrist. Describe the carpal tunnel and ulnar canal, including the structures that course through each. Explain the clinical presentation and anatomical basis for Dupuytren's contracture, carpal tunnel syndrome, and ulnar canal syndrome.

Question 3252
During a carpal tunnel release the surgeon takes particular care at the lateral end of the incision, where the skin of the thenar eminence is reflected. Question 3253
A patient asks how cutting a single band at the wrist can relieve pressure on a nerve when nothing is removed from inside the tunnel. Which of the following best explains the effect of the operation?
A. Dividing the roof allows the carpal bones to spread and deepens the floor

Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Carpal Tunnel Release; Flexor Retinaculum and the Contents of the Carpal Tunnel
Why this is correct:
The tunnel is a fibro-osseous space whose only yielding wall is the retinaculum. Dividing that band lets the nine tendons and the nerve spread, which takes the pressure off the median nerve without removing anything.
Why the other answers are wrong:

Question 3254

Question 3255
A student is asked to name the two structures that pass through the fibro-osseous arch stretching between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate. Which of the following pairs is most likely correct?

MSK / Week 15 / Wrist and Palm of Hand
Question 3256
A 46-year-old woman underwent an uncomplicated carpal tunnel release six weeks ago for hand numbness. Her symptoms are unchanged. On examination sensation is reduced over the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger, and she cannot spread her fingers apart. Which of the following best explains why the operation did not help her?
A. The flexor retinaculum was divided only partially
B. The affected nerve was compressed by an anteriorly dislocated lunate

Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Ulnar Canal and Ulnar Canal Syndrome; Flexor Retinaculum and the Contents of the Carpal Tunnel
Why this is correct:
Her sensory loss over the medial one and a half digits and her loss of finger abduction are ulnar. The ulnar nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum through the ulnar canal, so dividing the retinaculum does nothing for it.
Why the other answers are wrong:

B. That mechanism compresses the median nerve inside the tunnel, not the nerve affected here.

E. Her symptoms were unchanged from the start rather than recurring after a period of relief.

Question 3257

Question 3265
A 48-year-old man sustains a laceration of the ulnar nerve at the wrist. Which of the following lumbrical muscles would be expected to retain their function?

MSK / Week 15 / Wrist and Palm of Hand
Question 3266
A 53-year-old man is asked to hold a sheet of paper between his thumb and the side of his index finger while the examiner pulls it away. On the affected side his thumb flexes sharply at the interphalangeal joint in order to keep hold of the paper. Which of the following best explains that substitution?
A. Flexor pollicis brevis is recruited because opponens pollicis is paralysed
B. Abductor pollicis brevis is recruited because the first dorsal interosseous is paralysed
C. Flexor pollicis longus is recruited because adductor pollicis is paralysed
D. The first palmar interosseous is recruited because flexor pollicis longus is paralysed
E. Opponens pollicis is recruited because the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis is paralysed
Answer: C. Flexor pollicis longus is recruited because adductor pollicis is paralysed
Order: Third
Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Adductor Pollicis and Froment Sign; Movements of the Thumb
Why this is correct:
This is Froment sign. A patient with an intact adductor pollicis holds the paper with the thumb flat and the nail at a right angle to the palm. When that ulnar supplied muscle is lost, the median supplied flexor pollicis longus substitutes, and the thumb flexes at the interphalangeal joint to grip.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Flexor pollicis brevis acts at the metacarpophalangeal joint, and opponens pollicis loss does not produce this sign.
B. Abduction would move the thumb away from the paper rather than grip it.
D. The movement seen is interphalangeal flexion, which is exactly what flexor pollicis longus produces.
E. Opposition rotates the thumb rather than flexing its interphalangeal joint.
Objective: Define intrinsic muscles of the hand, their attachments, actions, and innervation. Compare & contrast the intrinsic muscles with the extrinsic muscles of the hand.

Question 3271
A 54-year-old man cannot keep a sheet of paper gripped between adjacent fingers when the examiner pulls it away, yet he can still spread the same fingers apart against resistance. Which of the following muscle groups is selectively weak?
A. Dorsal interossei
B. Lumbricals of digits 4 and 5
C. Palmar interossei
D. Hypothenar muscles
E. Adductor pollicis
Answer: C. Palmar interossei
Order: Third
Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Interosseous Muscles and How They Are Tested
Why this is correct:
Holding a sheet of paper between adjacent fingers against traction is the test of digital adduction, and adduction is what the palmar interossei do, which is the whole point of PAD. Spreading the fingers apart tests abduction, and that movement is preserved here.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The dorsal interossei abduct the digits, which is the movement he can still perform.
B. Those lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints rather than moving digits sideways.
D. The hypothenar muscles act on the little finger alone and could not hold a sheet between every pair of fingers.
E. Adductor pollicis draws the thumb toward the palm rather than adducting the fingers.
Objective: Define intrinsic muscles of the hand, their attachments, actions, and innervation. Compare & contrast the intrinsic muscles with the extrinsic muscles of the hand.

Question 3272
A 38-year-old man sustains a complete laceration of the median nerve at the wrist. He has no opposition of the thumb and wasting of the thenar eminence, yet he can still flex all four fingers fully at the interphalangeal joints. Which of the following best explains the preserved flexion?

C. The interossei take over flexion of the interphalangeal joints

Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Intrinsic Compared With Extrinsic Muscles of the Hand; Median Nerve Lesion at the Wrist
Why this is correct:
Extrinsic muscles have their bellies in the forearm, so the branches supplying them leave the nerve well above the wrist. A lesion at the wrist therefore takes the intrinsic muscles of the hand and leaves gross digital flexion intact, which is the whole logic of comparing wrist with elbow injuries.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral part of flexor digitorum profundus are median supplied.
B. The lumbricals extend the interphalangeal joints rather than flexing them.
C. The interossei assist in extending the interphalangeal joints along with the lumbricals.
E. Digital flexion is an active movement requiring the long flexors.
Objective: Define intrinsic muscles of the hand, their attachments, actions, and innervation. Compare & contrast the intrinsic muscles with the extrinsic muscles of the hand.

Question 3275
A 29-year-old man divides a band of fibrous tissue overlying the flexor tendon of his ring finger. Afterwards, when he flexes the digit, the tendon lifts away from the bone and bowstrings across the front of the finger. Which of the following structures was most likely divided?
A. Synovial sheath of the digit
B. Fibrous digital sheath
C. Extensor expansion
D. Palmar aponeurosis
E. Flexor retinaculum
Answer: B. Fibrous digital sheath
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Fibrous and Synovial Digital Sheaths
Why this is correct:
The fibrous digital sheaths are osseofibrous canals that bind the tendons closely to the phalanges and function as a series of pulleys. Dividing them allows the tendon to lift away from the bone when the digit flexes.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. That is a lubricating membrane and its loss would increase friction rather than allow bowstringing.
C. That lies on the dorsal surface of the digit and does not restrain the flexor tendon.
D. That lies proximal to the digit, in the palm.
E. That lies at the wrist and restrains the tendons as they enter the hand.
Objective: Identify and discuss the clinical importance of synovial sheaths & bursae of the hand.

Why this is correct:

Objective: Describe and recognize typical vascular patterns for arterial blood flow into the hand. Trace the sequential routes blood would follow in the hand.

Difficulty: Hard

The ulnar nerve is the motor nerve of the hand, supplying the hypothenar muscles, lumbricals 3 and 4, all the interossei, adductor pollicis and the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis. Why the other answers are wrong:

B. The radial nerve supplies no intrinsic muscle of the hand.
C. Those movements are produced by the interossei, which are intrinsic.

Answer: E. The long extensors and flexor digitorum profundus act unopposed on the digits
Order: Third
Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Ulnar Nerve Lesion at the Wrist and the Ulnar Claw Hand; Lumbrical Muscles
Why this is correct:
The lecture states that the claw is produced by the unopposed action of the extensors and flexor digitorum profundus. With the lumbricals and interossei gone, nothing balances the long extensors at the metacarpophalangeal joints or the long flexor at the interphalangeal joints.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. That is the mechanism of Dupuytren contracture, which is a separate condition.
B. The retinaculum is a fibrous band that does not contract.
C. Denervated muscle is paralysed rather than spastic.
D. The sheaths are pulleys and do not shorten to produce a deformity.
Objective: Discuss the clinical presentation and anatomical basis for significant hand/wrist problems including: fractures, dislocations, lacerations, ischemia, tenosynovitis, and neurological injuries.

Question 3315
A 45-year-old woman has an ulnar nerve lesion posterior to the medial epicondyle. Compared with a patient whose ulnar nerve was divided at the wrist, which of the following additional muscles would be expected to be paralysed?

Question 3316
A physician compares two patients with ulnar nerve lesions, one at the elbow and one at the wrist. Which of the following features would be expected to be the same in both?
A. The presence of radial deviation on attempted wrist flexion
B. The strength of flexion at the distal interphalangeal joint of the little finger

Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Ulnar Nerve Lesion at the Elbow; Ulnar Nerve Lesion at the Wrist and the Ulnar Claw Hand

B. The medial part of flexor digitorum profundus is lost only with a proximal lesion.

Question 3317
Two patients are photographed with the index and middle fingers extended and the ring and little fingers flexed. The first was asked to make a fist and the second was asked to open the hand. Which of the following best describes the lesions?

The two deformities can look identical in a still photograph and are separated by what the patient was asked to do. Benediction appears on an attempted fist, when the median supplied digits will not flex. The claw appears on opening the hand, when the ulnar supplied digits will not straighten.

Question 3318
A 44-year-old man has numbness of the medial one and a half digits and wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles. He can still flex the distal interphalangeal joints of the fourth and fifth digits normally, and his hand does not deviate when he flexes the wrist. Which of the following best explains both of those preserved findings?
A. The deep branch of the ulnar nerve has been spared
B. The median nerve has taken over the medial part of flexor digitorum profundus
C. The interossei are intact
D. Flexor carpi radialis has compensated for the loss of flexor carpi ulnaris
E. The lesion lies distal to the branches that supply the forearm muscles
Answer: E. The lesion lies distal to the branches that supply the forearm muscles
Order: Third
Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Comparing Median and Ulnar Lesions at the Wrist and the Elbow; Ulnar Nerve Lesion at the Elbow
Why this is correct:
Flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial part of flexor digitorum profundus both take their branches from the ulnar nerve in the forearm. An injury below those branches leaves both muscles working, so flexion of the fourth and fifth digits is unaffected and the wrist does not deviate on flexion, which places the lesion at the wrist rather than at the elbow.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The deep branch supplies the intrinsic muscles, which are wasted here, and sparing it would not preserve any forearm muscle.
B. The medial part of flexor digitorum profundus is ulnar supplied and the lateral part is median supplied, and neither takes over the other.
C. The interossei are lost at both levels, so their state cannot account for preserved forearm function.
D. Flexor carpi radialis is median supplied, and it is what draws the hand to the lateral side when flexor carpi ulnaris is denervated rather than compensating for it.
Objective: Describe the motor and sensory innervation of the hand. Trace the median and ulnar nerves and their branches within the hand. Compare and contrast their functions.

Question 3319
A 50-year-old man has numbness of the medial one and a half digits and weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles. The examiner wishes to decide whether the lesion lies at the wrist or at the elbow. Which of the following findings would place the lesion at the elbow?

Everything supplied in the hand is lost at both levels, so only a forearm sign localises the lesion. Radial deviation on attempted wrist flexion requires flexor carpi ulnaris to be denervated, and its branch leaves the nerve in the forearm, below the elbow.

MSK / Week 15 / Wrist and Palm of Hand
Question 3320
A 44-year-old woman has aching at the base of her thumb that is worse when she grips a jar lid. A radiograph of the hand and wrist is obtained and is shown. The joint she is describing lies between the first metacarpal and which of the following carpal bones?

A. Capitate
B. Hamate
C. Lunate
D. Scaphoid
E. Trapezium
Answer: E. Trapezium
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Carpal Bones, Their Rows and Their Articulations; Movements of the Thumb

The trapezium is the most lateral bone of the distal row and articulates with metacarpals one and two. Following the thumb metacarpal proximally on this film leads to a four sided bone sitting against it, which is the trapezium. That articulation is the one loaded during a forceful grip.

Question 3322
A 25-year-old is treated for the injury shown on this radiograph. He is warned that one part of the broken bone may die even if the rest of the bone heals. Which part is at risk?
![Radiograph](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-limb-197.jpg)
A. The proximal fragment
B. The distal fragment
C. The adjacent lunate
D. The adjacent trapezium
E. The distal end of the radius
Answer: A. The proximal fragment
Order: Third
Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Fracture of the Scaphoid
Why this is correct:
The blood supply to the scaphoid enters the bone at its distal end and runs proximally within it. A break across the waist therefore cuts off the proximal fragment from its supply, and that fragment is the one that undergoes avascular necrosis if the two parts separate.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The distal fragment keeps the vessels that enter the bone and remains perfused.
C. The lunate has its own supply and is not devascularised by this fracture.
D. The trapezium lies distal to the fracture and is unaffected.
E. The distal radius is a separate bone with an independent blood supply and is intact here.

Question 3326
A 34-year-old falls on an outstretched hand and is tender in the anatomical snuffbox, but the radiograph taken that day is reported as normal and he is sent home in a splint. Two weeks later the films shown here are obtained. Which of the following best explains why nothing was visible on the first film?
![Radiographs](library/images/msk-week-15/questions/q-ext-limb-194.jpg)
A. The injury began as a greenstick fracture and only later displaced
B. Soft tissue swelling in the snuffbox obscured the bone on the first film
C. The fracture line becomes visible only once bone resorption has occurred at its margins
D. The scaphoid is projected over the distal radius on a standard wrist view
E. The proximal fragment had not yet undergone avascular necrosis
Answer: C. The fracture line becomes visible only once bone resorption has occurred at its margins
Order: Third
Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Fracture of the Scaphoid
Why this is correct:
A scaphoid fracture may not show on a radiograph until 10 to 14 days after the injury, once resorption at the fracture margins has widened the line enough to be seen. That delay is why snuffbox tenderness after a fall on an outstretched hand is managed as a fracture even when the first film looks normal.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The lecture does not describe scaphoid fractures as greenstick injuries, and later displacement is not what makes the line appear.
B. Soft tissue swelling does not conceal a cortical break on a plain film.
D. The scaphoid is well seen on standard wrist views, which is why snuffbox tenderness directs the request in the first place.
E. Avascular necrosis is a late consequence of the fragments failing to unite, not the reason the line is invisible early.
Objective: Discuss the clinical presentation and anatomical basis for significant hand/wrist problems including: fractures, dislocations, lacerations, ischemia, tenosynovitis, and neurological injuries.

A 57-year-old man notices a firm lump in his palm and finds that one finger has begun to sit slightly bent. Sensation in the hand is normal. The palm is shown. Which structure has undergone the change responsible?

D. Involvement confined to the middle finger alone is not the described pattern.
E. The disease favours the ulnar side of the hand rather than affecting all digits equally.
Objective: Discuss the fascial structures of the hand & wrist. Describe the carpal tunnel and ulnar canal, including the structures that course through each. Explain the clinical presentation and anatomical basis for Dupuytren's contracture, carpal tunnel syndrome, and ulnar canal syndrome.

Answer: E. Eburnation
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Eburnation and the gross appearance of osteoarthritis
Why this is correct:

Why the other answers are wrong:

Answer: A. Stiffness for ninety minutes each morning that eases as she works

Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Rheumatoid arthritis: symptoms
Why this is correct:

Pneumonitis is one of the rare but important adverse effects of methotrexate, so a patient on the drug with new parenchymal lung disease has two plausible explanations.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Nodulosis produces subcutaneous nodules rather than diffuse parenchymal change.
B. Caplan syndrome requires nodules with pneumoconiosis.
C. Pleural disease collects fluid in the pleural space rather than producing this parenchymal pattern.
D. Felty syndrome is a hematologic complication.
Objective: List the notable extra-articular manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis
